title: A Practical Study of RISC-V Memory Architectures
summary: Examining how memory organization, controller behavior, and predictable interfaces shape efficient processor systems.

sections.heading: Abstract
paragraphs: This paper presents a practical study of memory architecture from the perspective of a small digital system. It focuses on the relationship between processor requests, controller state, buffering, and memory timing.
The study shows how explicit ownership and carefully defined read and write transactions make a memory subsystem easier to verify and extend.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Memory is not only a storage block. It is an interface between computation and the physical timing constraints of a digital system. A useful architecture therefore makes request ownership, response timing, reset behavior, and invalid operations visible.
RISC-V provides a clear instruction-set foundation for exploring these ideas because the surrounding memory system can be designed and tested independently of the processor core.

sections.heading: Methodology
paragraphs: The study models a controller as a finite-state machine with separate request, address, data, and completion signals. Small directed simulations are used to test read latency, write ordering, reset recovery, and back-to-back transactions.
The implementation is divided into interface, control, storage, and verification responsibilities so that each behavior can be inspected in isolation.

sections.heading: Results and Discussion
paragraphs: The structured controller model makes timing failures easier to localize. Buffering protects the storage interface from short bursts, while explicit state transitions make the waveform communicate the intended transaction sequence.
The main tradeoff is between simplicity and throughput. A small controller is easier to reason about, while higher throughput requires more overlap and more carefully specified hazards.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: A reliable memory architecture begins with a precise contract rather than with a large amount of logic. RISC-V-based systems provide a useful environment for applying this discipline to real hardware designs.
Future work can evaluate cache behavior, bus arbitration, and formal checks for protocol properties.

sections.heading: References
paragraphs: [1] RISC-V International, The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual.
[2] D. A. Patterson and J. L. Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design.

title: Design Practices for Reliable Digital Interfaces
summary: A structured approach to designing UART, SPI, and I2C interfaces that are easier to test, debug, and integrate.

sections.heading: Abstract
paragraphs: Digital interfaces fail most often at their boundaries: ownership, timing, reset, and error handling. This paper presents a practical checklist for making those boundaries explicit before implementation.
The approach combines protocol tables, targeted simulations, and observable status signals to reduce the cost of integration debugging.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: UART, SPI, and I2C are simple to describe but can be surprisingly subtle in a complete embedded system. A correct implementation must account for both the normal transfer and the moments when a device is late, reset, disconnected, or asked to process invalid data.
Writing the interface contract first gives hardware and software contributors a shared reference.

sections.heading: Methodology
paragraphs: Each interface is described using a timing diagram, ownership table, reset rule, and error response. Tests then isolate one rule at a time, such as UART framing, SPI chip-select timing, or I2C acknowledgement behavior.
Assertions and waveform inspection are used together so that a passing transaction is also understandable to the engineer reviewing it.

sections.heading: Results and Discussion
paragraphs: The interface checklist reduces ambiguous behavior during integration. Small tests expose protocol mistakes earlier than system-level demonstrations, where several independent failures can appear identical.
The method also improves documentation because each test becomes evidence for one explicit rule.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Reliable digital interfaces are built through precise contracts and focused verification. The same habits transfer across serial protocols and make future changes less risky.
The next step is to automate the protocol checks in a reusable verification library.

sections.heading: References
paragraphs: [1] N. W. Z. Schleicher, Digital Interface Design Notes.
[2] Official UART, SPI, and I2C device documentation.

title: From Embedded Prototype to Measurable System
summary: Investigating how microcontrollers, sensors, and software can be developed as small, testable system boundaries.

sections.heading: Abstract
paragraphs: Embedded prototypes become useful engineering systems when their assumptions, measurements, and failure modes are made explicit. This paper outlines a repeatable workflow for moving from a connected set of parts to a testable design.
The workflow emphasizes small interfaces, observable signals, and short measurement loops.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: A prototype brings hardware and software into the same feedback loop. Sensor behavior, power conditions, timing, and application logic can all influence one another, which makes a large first build difficult to diagnose.
A staged workflow keeps the system understandable while it grows.

sections.heading: Methodology
paragraphs: The proposed workflow begins with a signal and power map, followed by independent checks for the sensor, communication link, firmware state machine, and user-facing behavior. Each stage has one measurable acceptance condition.
Logs and repeatable test inputs are kept alongside the code so that a successful experiment can be reproduced after hardware changes.

sections.heading: Results and Discussion
paragraphs: Separating the prototype into measurable boundaries makes faults easier to classify. A communication problem can be distinguished from a sensor problem before both are hidden inside application behavior.
The cost is a little more setup at the beginning, but the saved debugging time increases as the design becomes more complex.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Embedded development benefits from the same engineering discipline as larger digital systems: define contracts, observe behavior, and test one assumption at a time.
This provides a practical foundation for reliable IoT and microprocessor applications.

sections.heading: References
paragraphs: [1] J. Axelson, Embedded Ethernet and Internet Complete.
[2] Manufacturer datasheets and application notes for selected sensors and microcontrollers.
